opus-5.5.text:
I think it helps to separate the two cases, because they fail in different ways as the decoding length grows.

For hybrid attention, meaning you interleave some linear attention or state-space layers with a few full softmax attention layers, the efficiency story is a bit misleading at very long lengths. People like to say "only a quarter of my layers are full attention, so I'm much cheaper." That's true at moderate lengths. But asymptotically, the full attention layers still have a KV cache that grows linearly with sequence length, and per-token decoding cost grows with it. As you push to hundreds of thousands or millions of tokens, those few global layers dominate both memory and latency. You've reduced the constant factor, but you haven't changed the scaling. So for long reasoning traces or agentic rollouts that keep extending, hybrid models eventually hit the same memory-bandwidth wall as a standard Transformer, just later.

There's also a subtler modeling issue. In a hybrid, the linear layers tend to become "local" workers, and the model leans on the softmax layers for precise retrieval. That works well, but it means retrieval capacity is concentrated in a few layers. It's not obvious that this division of labor stays balanced when the context becomes extremely long, and we don't yet have a clean understanding of the ratio and placement you need as length scales.

For all-sparse attention, where every layer attends to a selected subset of tokens using top-k selection, block selection, or learned routing, the main appeal is that compute per step can stay roughly bounded. But memory usually doesn't. You still keep the full KV cache around, because you don't know in advance which tokens will be needed later. So you save FLOPs but not storage, and at long decoding lengths storage and memory movement are often the real bottleneck. Unless you offload to CPU or disk, which brings its own latency problems.

The second issue with sparse attention is the selection step itself. To decide which tokens to attend to, you need some scoring mechanism over the whole history, even a cheap compressed one. That cost still grows with length. And selection errors compound in long generation. If the model misses a relevant token at step 50,000, it doesn't really have a way to recover it. Dense attention is forgiving because everything is always visible. Sparse attention bets that the important information is identifiable ahead of time, and that bet gets harder the longer the context.

So my overall view is that both are pragmatic, engineering-friendly compromises, and they work very well right now. But neither fully solves the long-decoding problem. Hybrid keeps a linearly growing state in some layers. Sparse keeps a linearly growing cache and relies on retrieval heuristics. This is why I think it's still worth pushing on the fixed-state side, building recurrent or linear-attention layers that are much more expressive in how they write to and update memory, like the delta-rule family. Ultimately, I think the answer will be some combination: a strong fixed-size memory that does most of the work, plus a small, carefully managed amount of exact retrieval, rather than simply stacking the existing options together.

r001.rationale: The response says the full-attention layers in a hybrid retain a KV cache that grows with sequence length and eventually dominate memory and latency.

r002.rationale: It identifies storage and memory movement from the full KV cache as bottlenecks for all-sparse attention at long decoding lengths.

r003.rationale: It explicitly states that all-sparse attention usually keeps the full KV cache, so it saves compute but not storage.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that both approaches are compromises, and the compromises show up in different places as the decoding horizon grows.

Start with hybrid attention, where you interleave a few full-attention layers with linear-attention or state-space layers. The appeal is that the linear layers give you constant memory and constant per-token cost, so the KV cache grows with only the handful of softmax layers. But that's also where the limitation sits. Those few full-attention layers are still doing all of the exact retrieval work. As the sequence stretches into the hundreds of thousands or millions of tokens, their KV cache is the thing that dominates memory again, and the ratio you picked at training time, say one in seven or one in eight, starts to feel arbitrary. You tuned it for a certain length regime, and at a much longer regime the linear layers are saturated while the full layers are strained. There's also a subtler issue: the linear layers have a fixed-size state, so no matter how clever the gating or the delta-rule update, the information they can hold is bounded. Beyond some horizon they're effectively doing lossy compression, and the model has to learn to lean on the full-attention layers for anything precise. That works, but it means the full layers become a bottleneck for both quality and cost precisely when decoding gets long.

All-sparse attention has a different failure mode. There you keep the full KV cache conceptually, but each query only looks at a selected subset. The memory still grows linearly with length, so you haven't solved the storage problem, you've just made the compute per token sublinear. During decoding that matters a lot, because decoding is memory-bandwidth bound, and you are still paging through a huge cache or doing some selection step over it. If the selection is learned, like block-level or top-k selection, the selector itself has to be cheap and accurate, and accuracy tends to degrade as the number of candidate blocks grows. Mistakes in selection are silent. The model just doesn't see the token it needed, and there's no soft fallback. If the pattern is fixed, sliding window plus some global tokens, then you've essentially put a hard cap on what the model can recover, and in practice you're relying on information having been propagated layer by layer, which is fragile.

So the way I think about it: hybrid trades exactness in most layers for a small number of expensive exact layers, and the limitation is that those few layers carry all the weight at long lengths. Sparse trades exactness per step for coverage of the whole history, and the limitation is that the cache never shrinks and the selection becomes the weak link. Neither one gives you both constant memory and reliable long-range retrieval.

What I find promising is thinking of them as two ends of the same spectrum rather than competitors. A fixed-size state is just extreme compression. Sparse attention is just a very expressive, very expensive state. The interesting middle ground is giving the recurrent state more capacity and better update rules, so it stops being purely lossy, while keeping some mechanism for exact lookup that doesn't require touching the whole history. I think where decoding length really explodes, the models that work will be the ones where the architecture itself learns what to keep and what to forget, rather than us hard-coding the ratio or the sparsity pattern ahead of time.

r001.rationale: The response says the few full-attention layers dominate memory as length grows and become a bottleneck for quality and cost.

r002.rationale: It identifies paging through a huge KV cache and the selection step as decoding bottlenecks for all-sparse attention.

r003.rationale: It explicitly states that memory still grows linearly with length and that sparse attention has not solved the storage problem.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is how much work still grows with the context length. With hybrid attention, you might make most layers sparse or use a cheaper attention mechanism, but the remaining full-attention layers still have to read an increasingly large KV cache. As decoding length grows, those layers can become the bottleneck. So you improve the constant factor, but you don’t completely remove the scaling problem.

All-sparse attention can go further, but then the challenge is deciding what to attend to. If you keep the attention budget fixed, you’re selecting a smaller fraction of the history as the context grows, and you risk missing information that matters. If you increase that budget to preserve quality, you give back some of the efficiency. And if finding the relevant tokens requires scanning the entire history, the selection process itself becomes expensive.

So I’d assess both approaches along two dimensions: end-to-end decoding cost and the ability to retrieve useful information from a growing history. Sparsity alone doesn’t guarantee either efficient decoding or reliable long-context reasoning.

r001.rationale: It says the remaining full-attention layers must read an increasingly large KV cache and can become the bottleneck as decoding length grows.

r002.rationale: It discusses the cost of selecting relevant tokens, including scanning the history, but does not identify KV-cache management as a bottleneck for all-sparse attention.

r003.rationale: It does not state that all-sparse attention leaves KV-cache storage requirements unreduced.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is whether the efficiency gains hold as the context keeps growing. With hybrid attention, you reduce how often you use full attention, but the remaining full-attention layers still have to read an increasingly large KV cache. So you improve the constant factor without fully removing the long-context bottleneck.

With all-sparse attention, you can limit how many tokens each decoding step attends to, but then selecting the right tokens becomes critical. If the selection process has to scan the whole history, that introduces its own growing cost. If you use a fixed local window or a restricted pattern, you risk missing relevant information far back in the context.

So I’d look at both latency and quality as decoding length increases. Can the method keep its memory access and selection overhead under control, and can it still retrieve the information it needs? A speedup at one context length doesn’t necessarily answer either question.

r001.rationale: It says the remaining full-attention layers must read an increasingly large KV cache, leaving the long-context bottleneck in place.

r002.rationale: It identifies token-selection scanning cost and potential retrieval quality problems for all-sparse attention, but does not say KV-cache management may become its bottleneck.

r003.rationale: It discusses limiting attended tokens but does not state that all-sparse attention leaves KV-cache storage requirements unreduced.
